assessment:
In this study, Huang and colleagues address a long-standing question in cerebellar neuroscience: whether individual granule cells receive inputs from multiple precerebellar nuclei (multimodal) or from a single source (unimodal). This distinction has profound implications for understanding cerebellar computation, as multimodal convergence was a key prediction of the influential Marr-Albus theory of cerebellar function. The authors employ an innovative combination of mouse genetics, viral tracing, and high-resolution confocal microscopy to map the convergence of two specific pathways—proprioceptive inputs from the external cuneate nucleus (ECN) and motor-related inputs from the basilar pontine nucleus (BPN)—onto individual granule cells across the entire cerebellar cortex.

The key findings are compelling and well-supported by the data. Using a newly generated Slc17a7-IRES-Cre mouse line combined with Cre-dependent viral reporters, the authors achieve selective labeling of ECN and BPN mossy fibers. By crossing this line with a TCGO transgenic mouse that sparsely labels granule cells, they can trace individual granule cell dendrites and identify their presynaptic partners at synaptic resolution. The study demonstrates that 40% of proprioceptive granule cells receive convergent inputs from both ECN and BPN pathways, providing the first direct anatomical evidence for multimodal convergence in mammalian cerebellar granule cells. Furthermore, the authors provide a comprehensive map showing that this convergence exhibits striking regional specificity: some areas (medial vermis) maintain segregated pathways, others show mixed populations, and certain 'hotspot' regions (paramedian lobule, paraflocculus, Crus2) are dominated by convergent granule cells. Additional experiments using retrograde rabies tracing and anterograde labeling from forelimb motor cortex (M1) suggest that the convergent BPN inputs carry motor cortical corollary discharges, supporting the hypothesis that these multimodal granule cells integrate motor commands with proprioceptive feedback.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is convincing, with appropriate methodology and rigorous quantification. The anatomical tracing is validated across multiple animals and independent annotators, demonstrating reproducibility. However, reviewers identified several areas requiring additional detail or clarification. The characterization of the Slc17a7-IRES-Cre and TCGO mouse lines is described too briefly, with insufficient information about specificity, efficacy, and whether TCGO labeling represents a stochastic sample or a specific granule cell subtype. The experiment demonstrating M1 input to paramedian-projecting BPN neurons (Figure 6) is of significant interest but lacks quantification and detailed description of reproducibility. Most importantly, while the anatomical convergence is well-established, the authors' interpretation of the functional implications—particularly the proposal that convergence enables conversion of motor signals to sensory coordinates—is speculative and not fully persuasive, as reviewers note that convergence at the granule cell level may actually limit independent adjustment of modality weights by Purkinje cell plasticity.

Despite these limitations, this work makes an important contribution to cerebellar neuroscience by resolving a decades-old debate about granule cell input structure and providing the first comprehensive map of multimodal convergence across cerebellar cortex. The findings have significant implications for understanding cerebellar computation and motor control, particularly regarding how the cerebellum might implement forward models by integrating corollary discharge and sensory information. The study establishes a foundation for future investigations into the functional consequences of multimodal convergence and the diversity of granule cell input patterns across different cerebellar regions.
